newsitem.title: UK: International LPG demand best in Asia, Europe quiet.
newsitem.headline: International LPG demand best in Asia, Europe quiet.

text.p: An interest in butane buying for petrochemical use in Japan and strengthening prices in China as demand continues to rise, gave focus to international Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) markets this week, dealers said.

But while East Asian interest picked up, Europe remained becalmed. Portuguese propane buying was the only focus of buying, propping up prices on the coasters, but large cargoes of both propane and butane sagged as naphtha and LPG fell.
A Japanese trader said that petrochemical buying for butane came back into the market, and that a recent deal was done at around $200 a tonne C+F Japan on a fixed price basis.
He added that current expectations are that the Saudi Contract Price (CP), the main benchmark for LPG in the East, will be set at around $185 a tonne for butane in May.

Spot price talk for May was around CP -$10/-$5 a tonne fob Saudi Arabia, he said, giving a notional fob price of $175-$180 a tonne. Freight from the Middle East Gulf to Japan was around $20 a tonne, so the price for May delivery was seen close to $200 a tonne C+F Japan.
Demand of propane and butane into China increased at stronger prices. "The Chinese market is getting firmer, so the discount to the AG will be reducing," said a trader.
But elsewhere in the region buying remained thin.
The Korea Petroleum Development Corp published data during the week which showed South Korea's propane stocks stood at 974,000 barrels in February, up from 701,000 barrels in February 1996.
Butane stocks were also up slightly, to 573,000 barrels in February from 548,000 barrels the year before.

This comfortable stock cushion has taken urgency out of Korean demand, and a trader said that there was still a long time before the country needed to return to the market for a stock build ahead of winter.

In the Middle East, there were rumours that the T2 tender, the second of three Saudi monthly spot tenders which play a role in setting the CP, had been awarded at $170 a tonne for propane and $182-$183 a tonne for butane.
A trader said that Abu Dhabi's Adgas had a selling tender closing on April 21 for 31.5 kt of propane and 13.5 kt of butane, and added that Saudi Aramco's T3 tender closes on the same date.
Aramco is offering 8.5kt to 12.5kt of both propane and butane.
Europe was the least exciting market.
"It's been completely quiet this week," said a Scandinavian trader. "The North Sea is balanced."
He said that all North Sea LPG availabilities for April have already been traded, and there have recently been some attempts to optimise and exchange cargoes, "only to some extent successful."
There was North Sea material still available in the first half of May, but some May terminal programmes have yet to appear, making companies reluctant to commit themselves too far forward.
Prices have fallen in line with losses on alternative petrochemical feedstock naphtha, which came down significantly over the week.
As a result, dealers believed that LPG must fall still further to maintain its differential below naphtha and become an attractive feedstock again.
One said that both propane and butane were at parity, with the level seen in the $160's a tonne cif NWE.
The Mediterranean was also quiet.
"We have a lull," agreed a trader from the region's largest seller, Algerian Sonatrach.
There was some propane demand from the eastern Mediterranean, especially Turkey, but the major western users -- Spain, France and Italy -- were seen as covered and effectively out of the market.
Butane was weaker still.
"There's so much butane on the market," said a would-be seller, adding that the price on a cif Lavera basis was now no better than the $160's a tonne as demand evaporated.
The only bright spot in Europe was the propane coaster market in the north, as players looked to build cargoes for Portugal.
"If you can meet Portuguese spec, the price is in the high $180's, even the low $190's," said a coaster trader. "If not, you'd be lucky to get $165 or $170.".
Butane coasters, by contrast, saw no such support.

"Butane's starting to come out of everybody's terminal and nobody really wants it. It's starting to come off," said the trader, adding that "you'd be struggling to get $145" (a tonne) for it on Friday.
In the U.S., trade was quiet, with prices largely tracking Nymex crude.
"There's no direction in the market," said a trader on the Mont Belvieu, Texas market, adding "there's no inordinate demand."
---Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom, +44 171 542 6412 (c) Reuters Limited 1997
